  Councilmember Pierson confirmed he and Councilmember Uhring agreed on some

  Contract Planner Smith stated reduced noticing and Farmers Market were new

  In response to Contract Planner Smith, Councilmember Uhring stated his only

  neighborhoods where they did not belong.

  Councilmember Pierson stated he agreed with a Major TUP for events over 1,000

  review process by the Planning Commission.

  In response to Councilmember Uhring, Councilmember Pierson stated serial events

  Councilmember Uhring agreed Major TUP would include such events as the Chili
  Cook-Off or Malibu Triathlon and would require Planning Commission review. He
  agreed serial events could be considered with Major TUP.

  Planning Director Mollica stated 10- and 21-day notice was required for

  Councilmember Pierson stated noticing was difficult for some art events.

  Councilmember Uhring stated the purpose of a TUP was to protect neighborhoods

  Councilmember Uhring agreed with the farmers market modification. In response

  Councilmember Pierson agreed with the farmers market modification. In response

  Zoning Ordinance Revisions and Code
  Enforcement Subcommittee Agenda Report
To:  Councilmember Riggins and Mayor Pro Tem Uhring

Prepared by:  Tyler Eaton, Assistant Community Development Director and
  Joseph Smith, AICP, Contract Planner

Approved by:  Yolanda Bundy, MS, PE, CBO, CFCO, Community Development

Date prepared:  March 20, 2026  Meeting date: March 26, 2026

Subject:  Beachfront Definition for Residential Development Standards –
  Local Coastal Program Amendment No. xx-xxx and Zoning Text
  Amendment No. xx-xxx

RECOMMENDED ACTION: Review the proposed definition of “beachfront” for
inclusion in the Local Coastal Program (LCP) Local Implementation Plan (LIP) and
Title 17 (Zoning) of the Malibu Municipal Code (MMC) and provide feedback for
consideration by the Planning Commission.

DISCUSSION: When applying development standards to projects requiring setbacks,
height, impermeable coverage, two-thirds calculation, and Total Development Square
Footage (TDSF), the LIP and MMC provide a different set of development standards
for “beachfront” and “non-beachfront” projects. Beachfront development standards
allow less setbacks and increased height than non-beachfront development
standards. Additionally, beachfront development is not subject to the impermeable
coverage, two-thirds calculation, and TDSF limitations that are otherwise applied to
non-beachfront development.

Neither the LIP or MMC provide a definition of “beachfront” or “non-beachfront” and,
while in most cases the distinction is obvious, there are nuances with the location of
development and configuration of some ocean-fronting parcels in the City that have
resulted in ambiguity for applicants, the City’s reviewers, and decision-makers. In
practice, the Planning Division and the California Coastal Commission through review

  Page 15 of 18
 of Malibu projects, have historically qualified that beachfront development standards
apply based on a parcel’s orientation to the coast, the zoning designation, and the
location of the structure; Geologic characteristics associated with the location of the
primary use structure, such as the footprint of a residence as it is situated on the parcel
is a defining factor, not just the location of the parcel. Establishing a definition of
“beachfront” in the LIP and MMC would provide clarity to the public and City, improve
consistency in project review, and reduce the need for case-by-base interpretations. It
would also better position the City if challenges to a project's design standards were
made by an applicant looking to maximize the extra code allowances of beachfront
development that are intended to be for the typical constrained beachfront lot.
Preparation of the beachfront definition was directed by the City Council on July 14,
2025.

Proposed Definition

The proposed definition would read:

  BEACHFRONT: A parcel is considered beachfront when one of its parcel
  boundary lines is the Pacific Ocean or beach directly adjacent to the Pacific
  Ocean, the parcel does not have a zoning designation of Rural Residential,, and
  the site of proposed development is either directly on the beach or within a low-
  lying shoreline area contiguous with the beach and not separated from the
  beach by a coastal bluff, cliff, hill, or other elevated coastal landform. Parcels
  not meeting these criteria shall be considered non-beachfront. Beachfront
  development standards shall only apply to parcels meeting this definition where
  the primary use structure is located in one of these areas. An ancillary structure
  on the beach shall not constitute a parcel to be beachfront if the primary use
  structure is not located on the beach.

The proposed definition would align LIP Section 2.1 (Definitions) and MMC Section
17.02.060 (Definitions) with the City’s practices for qualifying when beachfront
development standards apply. The structure of the proposed definition is characterized
by the following three components:

  1) Physical Relationship to the Pacific Ocean: A parcel must directly abut the
  ocean. This component is important to ensure beachfront development
  standards are applied to parcels adjacent to the coast and not parcels adjacent
  to other low-lying areas, such as lagoons or blue-line streams.

  2) Consistency with the General Plan: A parcel must not be located within the
  General Plan, zoning code, or LCP land use designation of Rural Residential
  (RR) due to the lower-intensity development pattern envisioned for the RR
  residential land use and minimum lot size of one acre. This component is
  important because several parcels in the City are designated as RR and are
  oriented along the coast, as well as typically being larger in lot size. These lots
  are typically larger in size and have development that is separated from the

   beach from elevated landforms covered in the paragraph below. Allowing the
  use of beachfront development standards for these large RR parcels along the
  coast could allow for the parcels to develop in a relatively dense pattern that
  would not be consistent with the rural ambiance envisioned by the General Plan
  for such areas.

  3) Geologic Characteristics of a Beachfront Environment: The footprint of the
  primary use structure of a parcel must be reflective of geologic characteristics
  of a beachfront environment such as representing a low-lying coastal landform
  contiguous to the beach and not being separated from the beach by a coastal
  bluff, cliff, hill, or other prominent elevated coastal landform. This component is
  important because some parcels in the City are oriented along the coast and not
  within the RR land use designation, such as parcels in the Single Family
  Medium (SFM) land use designation; however, the location of proposed
  development for a primary use is separated from the beach by a coastal bluff,
  hill, or some other prominent coastal landform. Typically, parcels that include
  coastal bluffs or other prominent elevated coastal landforms are also larger in
  lot size than the parcels that are reflective of a beachfront environment. Allowing
  the use of beachfront development standards for parcels along the coast that
  are separated from the beach by a coastal bluff or some other prominent coastal
  landform would allow for development much larger than intended by the General
  Plan.

Some of the key supporting General Plan policies from the Land Use (LU) Element
include the following:

  1) LU Policy 1.1.1: The City shall protect the natural environment by regulating
  design and permitting only land uses compatible with the natural environment.
  2) LU Policy 1.1.4: The City shall preserve the City's rural residential character.
  3) LU Policy 1.1.5: The City shall require careful site planning which blends
  development with the natural topography.
  4) LU Policy 2.3.2: The City shall discourage “mansionization” by establishing limits
  on height, bulk, and square footage for all new and remodel single-family
  residences.
  5) LU Policy 2.4.1: The City shall preserve and protect vistas and large open areas
  that contribute to the rural feeling of the area.
  6) LU Policy 6.1.1: The City shall use development standards and procedures that
  protect the property owners' reasonable use of their land consistent with the
  goals and policies of this General Plan.

Subcommittee Options

1. Recommend adoption of the proposed definition as drafted.
2. Recommend revisions to the definition language.
3. Request additional research before returning with a revised definition.
4. Recommend not to pursue the amendment.
